extracted.intended_audience: physicians/surgeons, lawyers, and informed public interested in medical-malpractice and professional-liability standards
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and legal standards for judging physician or surgeon liability: duty of care, patient cooperation, deviation from established practice, effect of assurances, and statutory licensing/registration requirements (with historical context).

rubrics_metrics.name: Duty to warn / give reasonable instructions
rubrics_metrics.description: Omission to give necessary warnings or instructions (e.g., to keep an arm at a right angle after treatment) may constitute 'culpable negligence' on the physician's part.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the physician omitted to warn the patient of an important post-treatment requirement and injury results, that omission is culpable. By contrast, if the physician performed skillfully and omitted nothing, but the patient neglected to comply, the surgeon's liability is limited. Example: failing to warn that the arm must remain in a particular position was held culpable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patient's duty to cooperate / contributory negligence
rubrics_metrics.description: It is the patient's duty to cooperate with the physician and conform to necessary prescriptions; neglect to obey reasonable instructions that contributes to the injury bars recovery.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contributory negligence is a valid defense. The patient who fails to follow reasonable directions (like a pedestrian walking on railroad tracks) cannot recover if his neglect contributed to the harm. Courts treat patient noncompliance as equivalent to contributory negligence in tort suits against physicians.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exception when patient relied on physician's assurances (reliance/inducement)
rubrics_metrics.description: If a patient neglected to use necessary precautions because lulled into a sense of security by the doctor, the doctor will be liable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where the physician's words or conduct induced the patient to relax necessary precautions, the patient's subsequent negligence will not bar recovery. This is an estoppel/reliance-based exception to contributory negligence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Refusal to submit to remedial attempts — effect on recovery
rubrics_metrics.description: A patient's refusal to permit an attempt to remedy injury already caused by malpractice does not necessarily preclude recovery if the refusal was made without reasonable assurance that the attempt would be successful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Nonconsent to further treatment will not always defeat a malpractice claim — especially if the proposed remedial attempt lacked reasonable assurance of success. The text also notes the view that refusal even after assurances might be 'just and proper' in some circumstances, indicating courts examine the reasonableness of the patient's decision in context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Weight of physician's assurances and guarantees
rubrics_metrics.description: Assurances from a negligent physician have uncertain weight; however, if the physician guarantees a successful issue, he will be held responsible in case of failure to effect a cure, even though ordinarily he would not be liable if he had merely employed due care and skill.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A physician's guarantee creates warranty-like liability beyond ordinary negligence standards. By contrast, mere assurances from a physician who has already breached implied obligations may be treated skeptically. Courts distinguish between ordinary standards of care and express guarantees of results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standard of care — exercise of care and skill
rubrics_metrics.description: Ordinarily a physician is judged by whether he 'employed such care and skill as were above spoken of' — i.e., the appropriate care and skill expected of practitioners.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a practitioner exercises the accepted level of care and skill in the profession, ordinarily he will not be liable for unfortunate results. This is the baseline negligence/standard-of-care rule underlying malpractice adjudication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deviation from established rules of practice (experimentalism) — strict English rule
rubrics_metrics.description: An English judge stated: 'Any deviation renders him liable.' This is a severe rule that would bar medical progress by forbidding deviations from established practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text criticizes the literal application of this rule as too severe because it would prevent progress; thus many jurisdictions temper it. It illustrates the anti-pattern of rigidly treating any deviation as negligence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deviation from established practice — American modification (when deviation is permissible)
rubrics_metrics.description: If physicians or surgeons have applied a different system of treatment and found it to succeed as well as or better than the one prescribed by authority, it is not negligence to resort to that system.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conditions for safe adoption of a novel or alternative treatment: (1) the system has been practically tested by others and found to succeed; (2) the cases in which it was tested are substantially the same as the present case; and (3) the treatment's success is such as to leave no doubt as to its propriety and safety. Otherwise, 'one can not become an experimentalist, except at his peril.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Latitude for physician in new, complex, or atypical cases
rubrics_metrics.description: When the case is new, or the injury/disease is attended with injury to other parts or other diseases have developed for which there is no established mode of treatment, latitude must be allowed the physician in the application of remedies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts will permit broader discretion where no well-established treatment exists; in such situations the patient must trust the physician's skill and experience. This is the exception to the requirement to follow established practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Departure from well-established treatment (risk borne by practitioner)
rubrics_metrics.description: When the diagnosis reveals a disease for which there is a well-established method of treatment, the practitioner who departs from it does so at his risk.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If an accepted, established treatment exists for a diagnosed disease, deviating from that standard exposes the practitioner to malpractice liability unless the deviation meets the safe-adoption conditions (see American modification).

rubrics_metrics.name: Liability categories for unlicensed practitioners historically
rubrics_metrics.description: Historically (in periods where 'quackery' prevailed), an unlicensed practitioner was liable only in cases of malpractice, gross ignorance, or immoral conduct in practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This historical standard contextualizes how courts treated unauthorized practitioners: they could practice but were subject to liability where conduct was grossly deficient. The passage contrasts this with later statutory efforts to require licensing and to penalize unlicensed practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory licensing prerequisites to practice medicine/surgery (New York 1874–1880 reforms)
rubrics_metrics.description: Statutes declared it a misdemeanor to practice medicine or surgery unless authorized by a license or diploma from a chartered medical school, state board of medical examiners, or medical society; later acts (1880) required practitioners to be twenty-one and to hold specified authorizations (licenses, endorsed diplomas, or prior authorization).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The statutes impose substantive prerequisites (age, diploma/license/endorsement) intended to drive out unlicensed practitioners and protect the public. The laws evolved from penal/criminal sanctions to regulatory schemes with fines and imprisonment for repeat offenses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Registration and affidavit requirements; penalties for false statements or illegal diplomas
rubrics_metrics.description: Physicians (with some exceptions) must register with the county clerk their name, residence, place of birth and authority to practice, and make affidavit as to the manner, date, and grantor of their license; willful falsity exposes the affiant to perjury and conviction. Violations or practicing under a diploma illegally obtained are misdemeanors punishable by fines/imprisonment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Procedural compliance (registration and truthful affidavit) is mandatory under the statute; failure carries criminal consequences and supports later disciplinary or penal actions. The text notes specific penalty ranges (historical): fines from $50–$200 (first offense), higher for subsequent offenses, or imprisonment (e.g., not less than 30 days).

rubrics_metrics.name: Exemptions and regulatory weak points (ten-year practitioners)
rubrics_metrics.description: The act exempted practitioners of ten years' standing from some provisions, creating a weak point that could leave a foothold for disreputable long-standing practitioners.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legislative grandfathering provisions aimed to spare established reputable physicians unnecessary trouble but risked allowing some disreputable long-standing practitioners to evade re-regulation. The text flags this as a statutory weakness in need of further reform.
